description: I'm Parv, a builder from India. I design and ship full-stack products with AI agents, and I like problems where the proof has to be real: live demos, receipts, tests that run. I work in TypeScript, Node, React, and on-chain systems. I'm interested in agents, payments, and tools that turn hard data into clear decisions.
summary:
Oneiric is a terrain-aware tool for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. For any site and date, it shows when a mission has sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth, from the real terrain horizon, LOLA elevation data, and Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons, hourly from 2023 to 2040. Each choice gets a verdict — GO, MARGINAL, or NO-GO — and the days of schedule slip it survives. Up to four sites compare side by side; 33 sites in all, with skylines at 0, 2, 10 and 20 m showing what a mast buys. A 3D Moon view shows all 33 sites on the globe.

Terrain decides both power and communications at the lunar south pole: a ridge 0.3 km away can hide the Sun for days, and a three-week slip can turn a good choice bad. A site-by-date matrix covers 33 sites over 120 days, so a planner re-evaluates in seconds after a delay, with no GIS training needed. In the worked case, de Gerlache Rim 2 is GO on 2028-09-05, NO-GO 21 days later at 28.3% sunlit.

Metres and degrees decide missions: IM-2 missed its target by 250 m, over 400 m by NASA's account, and ended about 13 hours after landing. Every number carries its source and a fidelity grade; the engine matches JPL Horizons to 0.00606 degrees at worst, skylines match known terrain to 0.00293 degrees at worst, and it replays six recorded mission events, including the 2025 eclipse to 0.2 minutes, the Blue Ghost landing, and Chang'e-6, where Earth never rises. No model sits in the computation path.
details:
Repo: https://github.com/parvagrwal/oneiric

Live app: https://oneiric-1jt.pages.dev/

What it does

Oneiric compares lunar landing sites and dates. For any site and any UTC landing date, it shows when a mission has sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth, from the real terrain horizon — and how many days of schedule slip that answer survives. Each choice gets a verdict: GO, MARGINAL, or NO-GO, plus the days it can slip later or earlier and stay viable, and the deciding rule in one sentence.

The library holds 33 sites — south-polar reference points, Artemis III candidate regions (each marked as an illustrative point, not a NASA-selected site), CLPS and international mission targets, and Apollo landmarks — plus custom latitude and longitude entry for any other point. Up to four sites compare side by side on one board, each with its own stay timeline, six metrics, energy figures and verdict, and a site-by-date matrix covers all 33 sites over 120 days (or 52 weeks), so a planner re-evaluates in seconds after a delay instead of starting over.

Twenty-four south-polar sites ship with terrain skylines at four observer heights — 0, 2, 10 and 20 metres, 96 skylines in all — showing what a mast buys before anyone builds one. A 3D Moon view shows all 33 sites on the globe with Sun and Earth pointers, and a south-polar map shows them against the terrain, with the nine Artemis region outlines.

When a stay goes dark or the link closes, the tool names the ridge that blocks it: its azimuth, how high it rises above the site, and how far away it is — and draws that ridge on the map. The Earth end of the link can be judged too, against four ground stations, and any instant can be checked live against JPL Horizons through the app's own proxy. Every control, site and date lives in the URL, so any scenario can be shared as a link, and each card exports its full 10-minute series as CSV and its scenario, metrics and sources as JSON. Five guided Explorer scenes walk a first-time user through the ideas with no manual, and a scripted 30-second Autopilot tour shows the Moon view, the scenario card and the matrix.

How it works

For each site the tool builds a skyline: the terrain's elevation angle in every compass direction, cut from LOLA elevation data. Rays are cast from the site across three tiers of elevation raster — 20 metres per pixel out to 15 km, 80 metres to 80 km, 240 metres beyond, out to 450 km — and each 0.25° of azimuth records the highest terrain and how far away it is.

Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, hourly from 2023 to 2040 in the Moon's mean-Earth frame, and their paths are drawn against that skyline. Sunlit time is computed from a 64-point model of the solar disc, including eclipses when Earth's disc covers the Sun, and solar energy is integrated over 10-minute steps at 1,361 W/m² for three geometries: a Sun-tracking vertical mast, a fixed vertical array (best of eight compass facings, with the facing printed), and a horizontal deck.

Verdicts come from editable stay rules — sunlit minimum, longest dark gap, Earth-visible minimum, longest link gap — evaluated every 6 hours over the stay, with gap edges refined to the minute.

GO means every rule passes with at least 3 days of late slip.

MARGINAL means every rule passes with less than 3 days.

NO-GO means a rule fails.

The stay presets are illustrative, not agency requirements: a 6.5-day sortie, a 14-day lander stay, and a one-year stay that reports annual figures with no verdict.

Every number carries its source and a fidelity grade: grade B means a complete 20 m near field, grade C means the 240 m raster only, grade D means a smooth sphere with no terrain, labelled as such and never shown as terrain. The engine is plain TypeScript, the same code in the data pipeline and in the browser's Web Worker, so the app and the checks cannot drift apart. No AI model is in the computation path.

The checks

The checks are part of the product, and the app shows them in its Method and checks drawer, rendered from the recorded results file. Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to 0.00606 degrees at worst across 8,000 comparisons (limit 0.02 degrees); the small Earth residual is the known apparent-vs-geometric difference, dominated by stellar aberration, verified by a frame-free check against Horizons geometric vectors. Skylines match known terrain to 0.00293 degrees at worst across 10,084 comparisons (limit 0.01).

The engine replays six recorded mission events:

The March 2025 eclipse, to 0.2 minutes.

The Sun hidden at the Blue Ghost site and back inside its allowed window.

The Blue Ghost sunset within its 3-hour limit.

The Chandrayaan-3 sunset 0.31 days after the sleep reference.

The Sun's azimuth swing at the SLIM landing site from 81.7 to 276.7 degrees as its panels caught the light again.

Earth never rising at the Chang'e-6 far-side site across 157,777 hourly epochs.

Against published figures, the engine reproduces Gläser et al. 2014 average illumination at four Connecting Ridge spots to within 0.15–0.62 percentage points. The test suite has 318 tests, and a mutation check plants 45 small faults in the engine and requires each one to be caught by a test. One check is still open: a cross-check against QuickMap, which has not been run and is listed as such rather than claimed.

What benefits it has

Terrain decides both power and communications at the lunar south pole, and a planner usually learns that from GIS work that takes hours and needs a specialist. Oneiric gives the answer in seconds, with no GIS training needed, and the answer is a number of days: how much slip a site-date choice survives.

The worked case shows why that matters. At de Gerlache Rim 2, a 21-day slip flips the verdict from GO to NO-GO, with sunlit time falling from 100% to 28.3% and the longest dark gap growing from zero to 110 hours, because a ridge 0.3 km away sets the horizon 7.17 degrees up — while the highest point of the same rim holds its GO and gains slip tolerance, from 4.25 days to 10.5. The tool found that pair by scanning 97,542 site-date combinations; it was not picked by hand.

The same comparison quantifies the mast: at Connecting Ridge the same stay is 36.8% sunlit at 2 metres and 100% at 10 metres, and at Shackleton Rim it rises from 0% to 73%. A planner can also see what blocks the light instead of guessing: at Connecting Ridge the Sun's dark stretch is traced to terrain 0.33 km away and 2.0 metres higher than the site. Every figure names its source and its fidelity grade, so a planner can trust the number or check it — and the checks themselves are shown in the app, with their limits, rather than hidden.

What I hope to achieve

A tool a mission planner can actually use when a launch slips: pick a site and a date, see the verdict and the slip it survives, and re-decide in seconds instead of re-running a GIS study. The method is open — the code, the data sources, the checks and the reproduce steps are all in the repository — so anyone can audit the numbers, reproduce them, or extend the tool to new sites, new observer heights, and new missions.

The aim is honest numbers for high-stakes dates: no figure without a source, no terrain claim without a fidelity grade, and no check claimed unless it was performed. The work that remains is in the same spirit: the QuickMap cross-check, skylines for the points of the 100 m landing circle once finer near-field data is available, and a horizon band once the elevation products' vertical error values are read — each one added only when it is measured, never estimated.

What it was built with

TypeScript throughout: the calculation engine, the React and Vite web app (with the engine running in a Web Worker), and the Node.js data pipeline. Three.js with React Three Fiber for the 3D Moon view, OpenLayers for the south-polar map, Tailwind CSS for the interface, geotiff.js for reading the elevation rasters, and the astronomy-engine library for the ground stations' Moon altitude in the browser.

The data is NASA public data, free with no key:

JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions (DE441 ephemeris, Moon mean-Earth frame).

LOLA south-pole elevation rasters from the Planetary Geodesy Data Archive (product 90; the 2.6 GB 20 m file is read remotely over range requests, never downloaded in full).

Moon Trek tiles for the map.

The NASA Scientific Visualization Studio CGI Moon Kit picture for the globe (orientation only, never used in a calculation).

The app is hosted on Cloudflare Pages, the code is on GitHub with continuous integration that runs the tests, the type check and the app build on every push, and the whole build cost $0 out of pocket. Code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5) and Muse, and the product requirements document was drafted with a sim.ai agent; no AI model runs in the calculation engine, and no AI-generated lunar imagery is used.
